clue.text: Ace coach Newcastle and England both ultimately mistreated

parts.note: A is the card abbreviation for ace
a coach is a long-distance bus

indicators.note: ultimately points to what comes last, so only the final letter of each named place is kept

parts.note: the final letter of Newcastle
the final letter of England

explanation.surface: A star football coach whose time with both Newcastle and England ended in being badly treated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both ultimately' applies the last-letter rule to Newcastle and England alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To abuse someone is to treat them cruelly, so abused is a synonym for mistreated.

clue.text: Like one of the lads, blow kiss as Connery says

indicators.note: Sean Connery's famous slushy S turns a sharp hiss into a 'sh' when he speaks

parts.note: blow kiss with the final S slurred as Connery would

explanation.surface: A macho type sends a kiss through the air the way Sean Connery would.
explanation.walkthrough: Connery's Scottish lisp, so often imitated, turns 'kiss' into 'kish'.
explanation.definitionFit: Blokeish describes laddish, matey behaviour typical of a bloke, that is, one of the lads.

clue.text: Most inclined, dearest

definitions.meaning: first meaning: having the sharpest slope

explanation.walkthrough: 'Most inclined' suggests the most willing, and 'dearest' the most loved; both are about slopes and prices instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep describes both a sharp gradient and an excessive price, so the superlative fits both.

clue.text: Reckless individual adjusting road speed

indicators.note: adjusting means changing the set-up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A daredevil driver who keeps changing speed on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless, often violent outlaw, so a reckless individual by definition.

clue.text: Maybe Edinburgh Fringe's iron lav — it's backed up

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: something backed up has moved in the reverse direction, so these words are read from the end

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A toilet at the Edinburgh Fringe is blocked and overflowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed up' suggests a blocked lavatory, but it tells you to read 'lav it's' backwards. The Edinburgh Fringe is the huge arts festival held each August.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edinburgh Fringe is one example of an arts festival, hence the 'Maybe'.

clue.text: As if Mrs Thatcher turned into a bearer of gifts!

indicators.note: turned into means transformed, so the letters are remade as something else

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Imagining Margaret Thatcher transformed into a generous present-giver, an unlikely change.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark points at the joke: Thatcher was hardly known for handing things out.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Christmas, the British name for Santa Claus, brings presents to children at Christmas.

clue.text: Defame upper-class Conservative entering commerce

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so these letters sit within the word for commerce

parts.note: trade is a synonym for commerce
U is the old label for upper-class usage
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Slandering a posh Tory who is going into business.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's 'U and non-U' distinction in English speech and manners.
explanation.definitionFit: To traduce someone is to speak badly of them and damage their reputation, a formal synonym for defame.

clue.text: Up in Llandudno, bag a V8 Rover

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, that is backwards
in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Llandudno, then bag, a and the V of V8

explanation.surface: Somewhere in the Welsh seaside town of Llandudno, a Rover car with a V8 engine is up for grabs.
explanation.walkthrough: Rover looks like the British car brand, but it is a wanderer. Llandudno is a resort town in North Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagabond is someone who wanders from place to place, which is what a rover does.

clue.text: "Is that Sondheim? It's Cyril, Dicky"

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for weak or unsound, so the letters are faulty and need setting right

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks if that's Stephen Sondheim; no, it's a man called Cyril Dicky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like Cyril's surname but is the anagram signal; Stephen Sondheim wrote the words for West Side Story.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Sondheim wrote song lyrics as well as music, so he is one example of a writer of lyrics.

clue.text: Small meteor explodes going over southern county

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small

indicators.note: an explosion scatters material in all directions, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: A little meteor bursts as it passes over a county in the south of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southern county' reads as one phrase, but southern belongs to the wordplay and joins meteor in the jumble; Somerset is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is one of the English shire counties, in the south-west of the country.

clue.text: A national treasure, casual runner not old but advanced!

indicators.note: 'not this but that' says one letter is dropped and another put in its place

parts.note: a jogger runs at an easy, unhurried pace
O is the abbreviation for old
A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A level

explanation.surface: A beloved national figure who jogs, who is not old but advanced in years.
explanation.walkthrough: The O of JOGGER is swapped for A. Mick Jagger, still running about on stage in his eighties, is the national treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Mick Jagger of the Rolling Stones is widely regarded as a British cultural icon, which is what national treasure means.

clue.text: Tiddles's tiddle very tiresome, in the end a sore point

parts.note: Tiddles is a stock name for a pet cat
tiddle is a childish word for a wee
V is the abbreviation for very

indicators.note: in the end keeps only the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: the last letter of tiresome

explanation.surface: The cat's wee is a terribly tiresome nuisance and, in the end, a source of irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiddles is the archetypal name for a household cat in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet peeve is a particular annoyance, the same idea as a sore point.

clue.text: Province that is pursued by Romeo?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the French-speaking Canadian province
second meaning: the code word for Q in the NATO phonetic alphabet, which comes just before Romeo for R

explanation.walkthrough: Romeo suggests Shakespeare's lover chasing someone; here he is the NATO alphabet's R, so what he follows is the code word for Q.
explanation.definitionFit: Quebec is both a Canadian province and the NATO radio code word for the letter Q.

clue.text: Painter's main view?

parts.note: surface reading: an artist's principal opinion or most important outlook
setter's reading: the main is the sea, so this is a painting of the ocean

explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like it means principal, but the main is an old poetic word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A seascape is a picture of the sea, literally a painter's view of the ocean.

clue.text: Cuddle rep when tipsy? That's not permitted

indicators.note: someone tipsy is unsteady and muddled, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Hugging a sales rep while drunk is against the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Precluded means ruled out in advance, so something precluded is prevented and therefore not permitted.

clue.text: Tea time conversation

parts.note: cha is a colloquial word for tea
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A talk over a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A chat is an informal talk, a synonym for conversation.

clue.text: Cabbage stuffed with cooked hake in mouth

indicators.note: stuffed with means filled with, so one word holds the other

parts.note: cole is an old word for cabbage, as in coleslaw

indicators.note: cooked means altered or tampered with, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cabbage dish filled with cooked fish, being eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cakehole' is British slang for the mouth, as in 'shut your cakehole'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cakehole is an informal British word for the mouth, the hole you put cake into.

clue.text: Changing key on end of Walküre, epic work by Wagner

parts.note: Alt is a key on a computer keyboard

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so just that is kept

parts.note: the last letter of Walküre
the Ring cycle is Wagner's four-opera epic

explanation.surface: A change of musical key at the close of Die Walküre, part of Wagner's vast opera cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface makes 'key' look like A to G; it is a computer key instead. Die Walküre is the second opera of the Ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Altering means modifying, a straightforward synonym for changing.

clue.text: Husband abandoning Wharton? Correct

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving behind, so one letter walks out of the name

parts.note: Edith Wharton was the American novelist of The Age of Innocence
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband leaving the novelist Wharton is the right thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Wharton is the surname; the solver must supply her first name, Edith, then drop its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to revise it, a verb synonym for correct.

clue.text: Reportedly, I look at various internet sites for items often raised

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, so the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.words: I look at various internet sites
parts.note: to browse is to look at various sites on the web

explanation.surface: Someone describing their web habits, looking at a range of websites.
explanation.definitionFit: People raise their eyebrows to show surprise or doubt, so they are items often lifted.

clue.text: Put in jail? No sir, Prime Minister, I got totally set up!

indicators.note: set up means arranged or framed, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
PM is the abbreviation for Prime Minister
taken as written

explanation.surface: A protest to the Prime Minister from someone framed and facing jail.
explanation.walkthrough: The framed protester is about to be jailed, so the clue reads as a whole as well as through its parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To imprison someone is to lock them up, the same as putting them in jail.

clue.text: Woo Betsey, oddly lacking politesse

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: lacking the odd positions throws away letters one, three and five, leaving the even ones

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of Betsey

explanation.surface: Someone courting Betsey strangely without any manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Courtesy and politesse both mean polite, considerate behaviour; politesse is the French-derived synonym.

clue.text: An island in the Med, Crete, evacuated in a whim

parts.note: Capri is an island in the Bay of Naples

indicators.note: evacuated means emptied, so only the outside letters of the word remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of Crete

explanation.surface: Choosing between Mediterranean islands, with Crete abandoned on a passing fancy.
explanation.walkthrough: Crete looks like the island the clue asks for; it only supplies its two outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A caprice is a sudden, impulsive change of mind, a synonym for whim.

clue.text: Free from former partner, almost completely drained

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
something completely drained is empty

explanation.surface: Getting free of an ex who has left you all but emptied out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free from' reads as one phrase, but 'from' only joins; the definition is just 'Free'.
explanation.definitionFit: Exempt means released from an obligation, so it is a synonym for free in that sense.

clue.text: A star, Liz regularly has food sent back home to Mozart

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the phrase is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of 'A star Liz'

indicators.note: sent back means returned the way it came, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: grub is slang for food

explanation.surface: A celebrity named Liz has her dinner returned to the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A star' looks like a separate clue piece, but it joins Liz as one string to take alternate letters from.
explanation.definitionFit: Salzburg in Austria is the city where Mozart was born and grew up.

clue.text: Boris — boundless spirit in the beginning

indicators.note: without bounds means without its edges, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: Boris without its outside letters
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, full of limitless energy from the start.
explanation.definitionFit: An origin is the point where something starts, a noun synonym for the beginning.

clue.text: Spooner's eaten small rodent in chaotic place

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words

parts.note: eaten is HAD and a small rodent is a MOUSE; swapping their opening sounds gives the result

explanation.surface: A pest has been eaten somewhere in a state of disorder.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of 'had mouse' to reach the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A madhouse, literally an old word for an asylum, is used figuratively for any scene of uproar and confusion.

clue.text: For example, Grand Hotel each day beginning to screen quiz show

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
Hotel is the NATO code word for H
ea is the abbreviation for each
D is the abbreviation for day

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of screen

explanation.surface: A grand hotel showing a quiz programme every day, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word here is an abbreviation; Eggheads is a long-running BBC quiz show where the public take on a team of quiz champions.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggheads is the name of a BBC television quiz programme, so it is an instance of a quiz show.

clue.text: Lab possibly admitting offence administering drug

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a Labrador is one kind of dog
a sin is a moral offence

explanation.surface: A science laboratory owning up to wrongdoing in giving medication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lab' looks like a laboratory, but it is short for Labrador.
explanation.definitionFit: Dosing someone is giving them a measured dose, which is administering a drug.
